stem: A ticketing company's Python service calls the Claude API with hand-written HTTP requests and its own retry loop. It breaks whenever a response contains a content block type the code didn't expect, and its retries hammer the API during outages. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Switch to the official Python SDK for typed responses, retries with backoff and streaming.
options.explanation: Correct. The SDK wraps the REST API with typed content blocks to narrow on, automatic retries with exponential backoff for retryable errors, and stream helpers, which are exactly what the hand-rolled client lacks.

options.text: Route the calls through an OpenAI-compatible shim so a more familiar client library can be reused.
options.explanation: A compatibility layer hides Claude-specific features and typed responses. The official SDK is the supported path when one exists for the language.

options.text: Keep the raw HTTP client but match on more strings in the response body to detect new block types.
options.explanation: String matching is the brittle approach that caused the breakage. New block types should be handled by type, as the SDK's typed unions do.

options.text: Generate a client from the API reference web pages once, then freeze it so behavior never changes.
options.explanation: A frozen home-made client still lacks retries and backoff, and it breaks again as the API adds fields and event types.

stem: A nightly shell script on a locked-down server must call the Messages API with curl, because no SDK can be installed there. It sends the API key and a JSON content-type header, but every request fails with a 400 error about a missing header. Which header is it most likely missing?

options.text: anthropic-beta, which every single request must send to choose a feature set
options.explanation: The beta header is optional and only opts in to beta features by name.

options.text: request-id, which the client generates so the API can trace each call
options.explanation: request-id is a response header that the API returns. Clients don't send it.

options.text: anthropic-version, which names the API version the request is written for
options.explanation: Correct. Raw HTTP requests must send anthropic-version along with credentials and the JSON content type. The SDKs set it automatically.

options.text: retry-after, which tells the API how long to wait before it may reply
options.explanation: retry-after is a response header on some rate-limit errors. Clients read it and never send it.

stem: A scouting tool sends several high-resolution scanned playbooks as base64 PDF blocks in a single Messages request. The request fails immediately with a 413 request_too_large error. The scouts still need Claude to read all the playbooks. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Retry the same request with exponential backoff until capacity frees up for the larger payload.
options.explanation: A 413 means the request exceeds the endpoint's size limit. Sending the same bytes again fails the same way.

options.text: Switch the request to streaming so the large payload is sent to the API in smaller chunks.
options.explanation: Streaming changes how the response arrives. The request body still has to fit within the size limit.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so the API reserves enough room to accept the larger set of documents.
options.explanation: max_tokens limits output. It has no effect on the maximum request size.

options.text: Upload the PDFs via the Files API and reference them by file_id, or split the work.
options.explanation: Correct. Request size is capped per endpoint. Uploading the files separately keeps the Messages request small, and splitting the work is another way to stay under the limit.

stem: A TypeScript developer wants each Claude request in a scoring-alert service to give up after one minute, so they configure the official SDK client with timeout set to 60. Every request now fails almost immediately with a timeout error. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The SDK requires streaming to be enabled before any timeout value is respected by the client.
options.explanation: Timeouts apply to non-streaming requests too. The issue is the unit of the configured value.

options.text: The TypeScript SDK reads the timeout in milliseconds, so 60 means 60 ms rather than one minute.
options.explanation: Correct. Timeout units differ by SDK: seconds in Python, milliseconds in TypeScript. One minute is 60000 in TypeScript.

options.text: Timeouts below the SDK's default are ignored, so the client falls back to an immediate cancel.
options.explanation: Shorter timeouts are valid and are applied as given. There is no fallback to immediate cancellation.

options.text: The API rejects requests from clients that set custom timeouts, returning a timeout-style error.
options.explanation: Timeouts are client-side settings that the API never sees. Nothing on the server rejects them.

stem: A league's partner webhook must respond within 30 seconds, and the handler calls Claude synchronously with the SDK's default client settings. During an incident, the handler hung for many minutes before failing, and the partner disabled the integration. The work behind each call usually takes 5–10 seconds. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Give this route a short per-request timeout and fewer retries, and queue slow work for later.
options.explanation: Correct. SDK defaults use a long timeout and retry twice, so wall-clock time can reach several timeouts in a row. A route with a hard deadline needs its own tight timeout and retry budget, with longer work handed off asynchronously.

options.text: Disable retries entirely across the whole application so no request can ever wait longer than one attempt.
options.explanation: Retries are valuable for other routes and transient errors. The fix belongs on the deadline-bound route, not globally.

options.text: Increase the SDK's maximum retries so transient failures are more likely to succeed within the handler.
options.explanation: More retries make the wall-clock problem worse. The handler would wait even longer before the partner's deadline.

options.text: Switch the handler to the Message Batches API so the partner gets its response from the batch results.
options.explanation: Batches are asynchronous with no response-time guarantee. They can't meet a 30-second synchronous deadline.

stem: A merchandise assistant's error handling checks whether the exception message contains the words "rate limit" and retries only in that case. After an SDK upgrade, the wording changed and rate-limit errors are no longer retried. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Catch the generic base exception and retry on every error, since any failure could be temporary.
options.explanation: Retrying 400, 401 or 404 errors wastes calls and never succeeds. Errors need to be told apart by type.

options.text: Parse the HTTP status code out of the error message text so the check is less sensitive to wording.
options.explanation: This is still string parsing. The SDK already exposes the status and a typed error class.

options.text: Catch the SDK's typed error classes, most specific first, before the general status error.
options.explanation: Correct. Typed exceptions are stable across message wording changes. Ordering from most specific to least keeps retryable and non-retryable cases distinct.

options.text: Pin the SDK to the old version forever so the error message wording can never change again.
options.explanation: Pinning blocks fixes and new features, and messages can still change on the API side. It treats the symptom, not the design flaw.

stem: During a design review for a live recap feature, an engineer states that receiving streamed output from the Messages API requires opening a websocket connection to the API. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The Messages API streams with server-sent events over plain HTTP, a one-way channel.
options.explanation: Correct. Setting stream to true returns server-sent events over HTTP. Websockets aren't part of the Messages API.

options.text: The Messages API streams over a websocket that the SDK opens and keeps alive between requests.
options.explanation: No websocket is involved. The SDK reads an SSE stream from a single HTTP response.

options.text: The Messages API can't stream, so clients must poll the request ID until the full response is ready.
options.explanation: The Messages API supports streaming directly. Polling applies to asynchronous work such as batches.

options.text: The Messages API streams over gRPC, so browsers need a proxy that converts it into websocket frames.
options.explanation: The API uses HTTPS with JSON and SSE. There is no gRPC interface to convert.

stem: A team building a fan-facing React app wants Claude's answers to type out live in the browser. A developer proposes putting the API key in the front-end bundle so the browser can stream directly from the API and skip the backend. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Ship the key in the bundle but obfuscate it, and rotate it weekly to limit exposure.
options.explanation: Anything shipped to the browser can be extracted. Obfuscation and rotation don't stop misuse of a leaked key in between.

options.text: Create a separate low-limit key for the browser so that leaks cost less money.
options.explanation: A leaked key is still usable by anyone until it's revoked. Lower limits only cap the damage.

options.text: Have the browser call the API directly but require users to log in before the key is loaded.
options.explanation: Once the key reaches the browser, any logged-in user can copy it and use it outside the app.

options.text: Keep the key on the backend, stream from the API there, and relay the text deltas to the browser.
options.explanation: Correct. The backend holds credentials and calls the API with the SDK's streaming support, then forwards deltas to the browser over SSE or a websocket. The key never leaves the server.

stem: A second-screen app streams Claude's play explanations to fans. Fans must be able to tap "stop" or send a follow-up while an answer is still arriving, and the app also pushes live game events to the same screen. Which architecture best fits?

options.text: Open a websocket from the browser directly to the Claude API and send stop and follow-up messages over it.
options.explanation: The Claude API doesn't offer a websocket interface, and calling it from the browser would expose the API key.

options.text: Use a websocket between browser and backend; the backend streams from Claude over SSE and relays events both ways.
options.explanation: Correct. The two-way need is between your browser and your backend, which is where a websocket fits. The backend keeps the key, consumes the SSE stream from the API, and can cancel it when a fan taps stop.

options.text: Have the browser poll the backend every second, and let the backend use the Message Batches API for answers.
options.explanation: Polling adds delay, and batches are asynchronous with no response-time guarantee. Neither fits a live experience.

options.text: Stream from Claude with SSE straight into the browser and handle stop requests by reloading the page.
options.explanation: SSE is one-way, and a reload is a poor stop control. The request also needs to go through the backend to protect the key.

stem: A backend relays Claude's streamed answers to browsers over websockets. Logs show that when a fan closes the tab mid-answer, the backend keeps reading the upstream stream to the end, and output-token spend for abandoned answers is significant. Which change best fits?

options.text: Lower max_tokens on every request so abandoned answers cost less when they run to completion.
options.explanation: This shortens every answer, including ones users read in full, and abandoned answers still run until the cap.

options.text: Buffer the full answer on the backend and send it only when it's complete, so tabs close less often.
options.explanation: Removing live streaming hurts the experience and doesn't stop generation for users who leave.

options.text: Treat a websocket disconnect as cancellation and abort the upstream stream from the backend.
options.explanation: Correct. When nobody is listening, the backend should close the upstream request instead of consuming a response no one will see.

options.text: Move abandoned conversations to the Message Batches API so the unfinished answers cost half as much.
options.explanation: A batch can't take over a stream that is already running, and the abandoned answers aren't needed at any price.

stem: A hand-written SSE parser in a sports-betting news service handles message_start, the content block events, message_delta and message_stop. It crashes intermittently in production on events it doesn't recognize. Which two changes best fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Skip ping events, which can appear anywhere in the stream and carry no content.
options.explanation: Correct. Streams may include any number of ping events. They should be ignored, not treated as errors.

options.text: Abort the stream on any event type the parser doesn't recognize, then retry the request.
options.explanation: New event types can be added over time. Aborting on them causes needless failures and repeated spend.

options.text: Retry the request whenever a ping event arrives, since it means the connection stalled.
options.explanation: Ping events are normal keep-alive traffic. Retrying on them would discard good responses.

options.text: Handle unknown event types gracefully, by logging and skipping them instead of throwing.
options.explanation: Correct. The docs say new event types may be added, so clients should tolerate events they don't recognize.

options.text: Switch to websockets, whose message framing prevents unrecognized events from appearing.
options.explanation: The Messages API streams over SSE. There is no websocket option, and the parser still has to tolerate new events.

stem: A live recap service checks the HTTP status of each streaming request and shows an error banner only for non-200 responses. During a traffic spike, some recaps freeze halfway with no banner, and logs show the HTTP status was 200. What is the most likely cause, and the best fix?

options.text: The SDK silently drops streams longer than its timeout; raise the timeout so recaps can finish.
options.explanation: Timeouts raise a client error rather than freezing silently, and the logs point to a server-side event, not the client timeout.

options.text: An error event arrived inside the 200 stream; handle it in the stream loop and retry with backoff.
options.explanation: Correct. Errors can arrive as events in a stream that already returned 200. The stream loop must handle them, for example by retrying with backoff and showing a retrying state.

options.text: The 200 status means the recap completed, so the frozen text must be a front-end rendering bug.
options.explanation: A 200 only means the stream started. The response can still end with an error event.

options.text: Overloaded errors are only ever sent before a stream starts, so the freeze must come from the network.
options.explanation: The API can send an overloaded error mid-stream, which in a non-streaming call would have been a 529.

stem: A long streamed season-review article on a current Claude model is cut off by a network drop after about 70% of the text has arrived. Regenerating it from scratch is slow and costly, and the partial text is saved. Which recovery approach best fits?

options.text: Send a new request with a user message that quotes the partial text and asks Claude to continue from there.
options.explanation: Correct. On current models, the continuation goes in a user message containing the partial response and an instruction to continue. Then stream the rest.

options.text: Send the partial text back as a final assistant message so the model continues it as a prefill.
options.explanation: That was the recovery pattern for older models. Current models reject assistant prefill with a 400 error.

options.text: Reconnect to the same stream with the last event ID so the API resumes from where it stopped.
options.explanation: The documented recovery for a dropped stream is a new request, not resuming the old one from an event ID.

options.text: Re-run the request with a higher max_tokens value, because the drop was caused by hitting the limit.
options.explanation: The cause was a network failure, not the output cap. A higher limit regenerates the whole article anyway.

stem: On NFL draft night, a team's trade-rumor bot expects traffic to jump from near zero to ten times its normal peak within minutes. Last year it hit a wave of 429 errors at the start. Which two practices best reduce 429 errors this year? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Retry each 429 immediately in a tight loop so requests get through before the surge peaks.
options.explanation: Immediate retries add load and make limits worse. Wait for retry-after and back off.

options.text: Ramp traffic up gradually ahead of the event instead of jumping from idle to peak.
options.explanation: Correct. Sharp increases in usage can trigger acceleration limits. Ramping up gradually and keeping usage consistent avoids them.

options.text: Create extra API keys in the same organization so each key gets its own rate limit.
options.explanation: Rate limits apply at the organization level, so more keys in the same organization don't add capacity.

options.text: Cache the large shared prompt prefix, since cache reads don't count toward input-token limits on most models.
options.explanation: Correct. With cache-aware rate limits, cached reads don't count against the input-tokens-per-minute limit on most models, so the same limit carries more traffic.

options.text: Switch every request from streaming to non-streaming, which is counted against a separate rate limit.
options.explanation: Streaming and non-streaming requests draw on the same limits. Switching doesn't create new capacity.

stem: A developer on a fantasy-sports team hardcodes the Claude API key into the source file of a new service so it works in local testing. The repository is shared with contractors. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Commit the key but restrict repository access to the core team members only.
options.explanation: Secrets in source control spread to clones, forks and history. Access restrictions don't remove them.

options.text: Encode the key in base64 inside the source file so it isn't readable at a glance.
options.explanation: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode the key.

options.text: Split the key into two string constants in different files and join them at runtime.
options.explanation: The key is still in the repository and can be reassembled by anyone who reads the code.

options.text: Load the key from an environment variable or secret store, as the SDK client expects.
options.explanation: Correct. A zero-argument SDK client reads credentials from the environment, so the key stays out of code and can be rotated without code changes.

stem: A league compliance job lists all of the organization's uploaded files to find documents older than a year. It reports only the first batch of results, even though staff know there are many more files. The job calls the list endpoint once and reads the returned array. Which change best fits?

options.text: Call the list endpoint repeatedly with the same parameters until the result count stops changing.
options.explanation: Repeating the same call returns the same first page. Pagination needs the cursor from each response.

options.text: Raise max_tokens on the list call so the API returns more items in one response.
options.explanation: max_tokens applies to Messages generation, not to list endpoints.

options.text: Use the SDK's auto-pagination when iterating the list so it fetches every page in turn.
options.explanation: Correct. List endpoints return pages. The SDKs' auto-pagination follows the cursors for you, so iterating yields every item.

options.text: Switch the job to the Message Batches API, which returns every file in a single result set.
options.explanation: Batches process Messages requests. They don't list files.

stem: A production assistant for a stadium-operations team occasionally fails, and the on-call engineer struggles to get help from Anthropic support or to correlate failures. Which two things should the client log for each failed API call? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The request ID the API returns with the response
options.explanation: Correct. Every response carries a request ID, also included in error bodies. Quoting it lets support find the exact call.

options.text: The full API key, so support can locate the account
options.explanation: Never log credentials. The request ID and organization details are enough to identify the call.

options.text: The SDK's default retry and timeout settings
options.explanation: Defaults are the same on every call and say nothing about why a particular call failed.

options.text: The HTTP status and the error type from the body
options.explanation: Correct. The status code and error type, such as rate_limit_error or overloaded_error, show whether the failure is retryable and where to look.

options.text: A count of the ping events received in the stream
options.explanation: Ping events are keep-alive traffic and carry no diagnostic value.

stem: A sports-data company writes its backend in Elixir, a language with no official Anthropic SDK, and wants to add Claude-generated injury summaries. The team asks how to integrate. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Call the REST API directly with the required headers, and add backoff for 429 and 5xx errors.
options.explanation: Correct. Raw HTTP is the right choice when no official SDK exists for the language. The team then owns what an SDK would provide, such as versioned headers, typed errors and retries.

options.text: Run the Python SDK in a subprocess for every request and parse its printed output back into Elixir.
options.explanation: A per-request subprocess adds latency and fragile text parsing. Calling the REST API directly is simpler and supported.

options.text: Use an OpenAI-compatible endpoint shim so a generic third-party client library can be used instead.
options.explanation: Compatibility layers hide Claude-specific features. The native REST API is available to any language.

options.text: Call the REST API directly but leave out the version header so requests always get the newest behavior.
options.explanation: The version header is required. Leaving it out causes errors rather than opting in to new behavior.

stem: A curl script calls the Messages API with the right auth, `anthropic-version` and content-type headers. The developer adds a request field for a feature that the docs describe as beta, and the request now fails with an error saying the field isn't recognized. What is missing?

options.text: A newer `anthropic-version` value, since every beta feature needs the latest API version
options.explanation: Beta features are opted into by name, not by moving the API version.

options.text: An `anthropic-beta` header naming the feature, which opts the request into it
options.explanation: Correct. Beta features are enabled per request with the `anthropic-beta` header. Without it, the API treats the beta field as unknown.

options.text: A different endpoint, because beta features live under `/v1/beta/messages`
options.explanation: Beta features are used through the same endpoint with an opt-in header.

options.text: Moving the field into the URL query string, where beta parameters are read
options.explanation: Request parameters go in the JSON body. The opt-in is a header, not a query string.

stem: A usage dashboard for a streaming recap service adds up the `output_tokens` value from every `message_delta` event in each stream. Its totals come out well above what the billing console shows for the same requests. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Streaming is billed at a premium, so the billing console under-reports streamed usage
options.explanation: Streaming doesn't change the price, and the console reflects real billed usage.

options.text: Each `message_delta` count is cumulative; use the final value instead of summing
options.explanation: Correct. Each count already includes the earlier ones. Summing them counts the same tokens several times.

options.text: `ping` events also carry token counts, and the code is missing them
options.explanation: `ping` events are keep-alives with no usage. Missing them would make totals lower, not higher.

options.text: The console only counts input tokens for streamed requests
options.explanation: Billing covers both input and output. The difference comes from how the dashboard aggregates.

stem: A club moves its Python stats assistant to Claude on Amazon Bedrock. A developer keeps the first-party `Anthropic()` client and only changes its `base_url` to the Bedrock endpoint. Requests fail with authentication errors. Which fix best fits?

options.text: Send the Anthropic API key in an AWS signature header alongside the new `base_url`
options.explanation: Bedrock authenticates with AWS credentials, not an Anthropic API key. Patching headers by hand rebuilds what the SDK's platform client already does.

options.text: Rewrite the integration as raw HTTP calls to Bedrock, since the SDK doesn't support cloud platforms
options.explanation: The SDKs ship dedicated cloud clients, so dropping to raw HTTP gives up typed errors, retries and stream helpers.

options.text: Use the SDK's Bedrock client, which handles AWS auth behind the same interface
options.explanation: Correct. Each platform has its own client with the right auth and model-ID handling, while the calling code stays the same.

options.text: Keep the first-party client and ask AWS to accept Anthropic API keys for the account
options.explanation: Bedrock uses AWS IAM. The fix is on the client side, by using the platform's client.

stem: A news site wants Claude's game summaries to appear word by word in the reader's browser. Readers never send anything while a summary is streaming; there is no stop button and no live input. An engineer plans a websocket service between browser and backend. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Relay the text deltas from the backend as its own server-sent event stream
options.explanation: Correct. When the browser only receives, re-streaming SSE from the backend is simpler than a two-way websocket, and the API key stays on the server.

options.text: Build the websocket service anyway, since streaming always requires websockets
options.explanation: Websockets are for two-way channels. This flow is one-way, and the Messages API itself streams with SSE.

options.text: Let the browser call the Messages API directly with a restricted key
options.explanation: API keys must never be shipped to the browser, whatever their scope.

options.text: Wait for the complete summary on the backend, then send it in one response
options.explanation: This gives up the word-by-word display the site wants.

stem: A high-volume highlights service wants to slow its own request rate before it starts receiving 429 errors, rather than only reacting after they arrive. Which signal best supports this?

options.text: The `request-id` header, which increases as the organization nears its limit
options.explanation: The request ID identifies a request for support. It carries no rate-limit information.

options.text: The monthly invoice, checked each morning to estimate the day's headroom
options.explanation: Rate limits are per minute. A billing view is far too coarse and too late.

options.text: The `anthropic-ratelimit-*` response headers showing remaining capacity
options.explanation: Correct. These headers show how much of each limit is left, so the client can throttle before hitting a 429.

options.text: Average response latency, since latency always rises just before a 429
options.explanation: Latency is an unreliable proxy. The API reports remaining capacity directly.

stem: A ticket-pricing assistant's nightly job suddenly fails every request with a 429 rate_limit_error. The response has no retry-after header, the error details carry the code enforced_spend_limit_reached, and the SDK's automatic retries keep failing. Traffic was normal all evening. Which response best fits?

options.text: Raise max_retries and the backoff delay so the job keeps on trying until enough capacity frees up again.
options.explanation: This 429 comes from the organization's monthly spend cap, not from per-minute capacity. Retries keep failing until access resumes, so more of them only burn time.

options.text: Treat it as the monthly spend cap: alert a human and raise the limit or wait for access to resume.
options.explanation: Correct. A spend-cap 429 has the same error type as a rate limit but no retry-after header, and its error code identifies it. It won't clear by waiting seconds; it needs a higher limit or the next billing month.

options.text: Spread the job's requests over more API keys in the organization so each key gets its own quota.
options.explanation: Spend caps and rate limits apply at the organization level, so extra keys in the same organization share the same cap.

options.text: Ramp the request rate up more gradually so the job stops triggering acceleration limits.
options.explanation: Acceleration limits come from sudden traffic spikes, and traffic was normal. The error code points to the spend cap, which no ramp-up will lift.

stem: A Python service that writes long season-preview reports raises max_tokens to a very large value. The official SDK now raises an error before sending the non-streaming request, saying it is expected to take too long. The service only needs the finished report, not live text. Which change best fits?

options.text: Catch the error and resend the same request with raw HTTP so the SDK check is skipped.
options.explanation: The check exists because long idle non-streaming connections can be dropped by networks and time out. Bypassing it with raw HTTP keeps the risk and loses the SDK's retries and typed errors.

options.text: Lower max_tokens back below the limit and split the report into several shorter, separate requests.
options.explanation: Splitting the report changes the product to work around a transport issue, and adds stitching and consistency problems. Streaming handles long outputs directly.

options.text: Raise the client's timeout to several hours, which also removes this error at the same time.
options.explanation: A huge timeout removes the error but keeps a long idle connection open, which some networks drop. The documented recommendation for long requests is streaming.

options.text: Use the SDK's streaming helper and collect the final message, since no live display is needed.
options.explanation: Correct. Streaming keeps data flowing on the connection, so long generations don't hit idle-connection drops. The SDK's stream helper can still return the complete message at the end.

stem: A nightly job submits 300 player-profile requests as one Message Batch, in roster order. When the batch ends, the job writes result 1 to player 1, result 2 to player 2 and so on. Some profiles end up attached to the wrong players. Which fix best fits?

options.text: Give each request a custom_id such as the player's ID and match results by that ID.
options.explanation: Correct. Batch results can come back in any order. The custom_id on each request is returned with its result, so matching on it is the reliable way to pair them.

options.text: Sort the results by their message ID before matching them up with the roster order.
options.explanation: Message IDs are not tied to the order of requests in the batch, so sorting on them doesn't restore the original order.

options.text: Send the 300 requests as 300 single-request batches so each result has only one owner.
options.explanation: This works around the problem at the cost of managing hundreds of batches. The built-in custom_id already pairs each result with its request.

options.text: Wait a few minutes after the batch ends so the results finish sorting into request order.
options.explanation: Results are not reordered over time. The documentation states they may not match the order in which requests were submitted.

stem: A Python async web server (asyncio-based) answers fan questions by calling Claude with the SDK's synchronous Anthropic client inside its request handlers. Under load, the whole server stalls while any single Claude call is in flight, even for requests that don't use Claude. Which change best fits?

options.text: Lower the client timeout to a few seconds so that each blocking call finishes much sooner.
options.explanation: A shorter timeout cuts off legitimate answers and still blocks the event loop for every call in progress. It treats the symptom, not the cause.

options.text: Replace the SDK with hand-written HTTP calls, because the SDK can't be used in async code.
options.explanation: The SDK has an async client with the same interface. Hand-written HTTP would lose retries, typed errors and stream helpers for no gain.

options.text: Switch to the SDK's AsyncAnthropic client and await its calls so the event loop stays free.
options.explanation: Correct. The synchronous client blocks the thread it runs on, which in an asyncio server is the event loop serving every request. The async client exposes the same methods as awaitable calls, so other requests proceed while one waits on Claude.

options.text: Set max_retries to 0 so that failed calls return at once instead of blocking all the other requests.
options.explanation: Retries are not what blocks the server; the synchronous call is. Removing retries only makes transient failures reach users more often.

stem: A recap service reads `response.content[0].text` to get Claude's answer. After the team enables thinking and turns on citations for its source documents, the code crashes on some responses and drops part of the answer on others. Which two changes make the response handling robust? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Turn thinking off on every request so the first block is always the text answer.
options.explanation: Some current models reject requests that disable thinking, and other block types can still come first. The code should handle the block list rather than force a fixed shape.

options.text: Iterate over the content blocks and narrow each one by its type before reading text.
options.explanation: Correct. Content is a list of typed blocks, such as thinking, text and tool use. Checking each block's type avoids reading text from a block that has none.

options.text: Read the last content block instead of the first, since the answer always comes last.
options.explanation: The last block can be a tool use block, and with citations the answer is split across several text blocks. Any fixed position is fragile.

options.text: Join the text of every text block in order, since one answer can span several blocks.
options.explanation: Correct. With citations, a response is split into several text blocks, some carrying citations. Taking only one block drops the rest of the answer.

options.text: Convert the response to a JSON string and extract the answer with a regular expression.
options.explanation: Regex over serialized JSON throws away the SDK's typed blocks and breaks when the structure or escaping changes.

stem: A stats-commentary service on Claude Sonnet 4.6 sends temperature 0.3 on every request. The team upgrades the official SDK to its newest major version and changes nothing else. Every request now fails with a 400 error, although the model ID is the same. Which two statements correctly explain or fix this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The model ID was silently pointed at a newer model that rejects sampling parameters.
options.explanation: A model ID names a fixed model and doesn't change underneath you. What changed is the API version the new SDK sends.

options.text: The new SDK major version sends API version 2026-10-21, which rejects sampling parameters.
options.explanation: Correct. Each SDK major version sends the API version that was current at its release. In 2026-10-21, any request that sends temperature, top_p or top_k returns a 400 on every model.

options.text: The 400 is a transient server error, so retrying with exponential backoff will clear it.
options.explanation: A 400 means the request is invalid. The same request fails again on every retry until it changes.

options.text: Stop sending temperature and steer consistency with clearer prompts, examples and validation.
options.explanation: Correct. The migration guide says to stop sending the parameter (or keep that request on the older API version for now). Without it, requests sample with the defaults, so consistency has to come from prompt design and checks.

options.text: Send temperature at its default value of 1.0 instead, which the new API version accepts.
options.explanation: In 2026-10-21 a sampling parameter returns a 400 even at its default value. The parameter has to be left out entirely.
